VISA Inc. Interview Experience
Darsh Shah · VJTI Mumbai
1. VISA Inc. — An Overview
Visa Inc. is an American multinational payment technology company headquartered
in Foster City, California (founded 1958). It operates one of the world’s largest electronic
payment networks across 200+ countries. Visa does not issue cards or extend credit
— it provides the infrastructure (the payment rails) that authorises, clears, and settles
transactions between financial institutions, merchants, and consumers.
Vision: “The best way to pay and be paid, for everyone, everywhere.”
Mission: To connect the world through the most innovative, reliable and secure
payments network.
Core Values: Integrity · Client Focus · Collaboration · Innovation · Excellence
VISA visited VJTI, Mumbai in October 2025 recruiting for the SWE Intern role.
The process had two stages — an Online Assessment (mid-October) and a Technical
Interview (23rd October).

2.1. Question 1 — Local Peak Indices
Easy · 20/20 TC
Problem Statement: Given an integer array arr, return a new array containing all
indices such that the element at that index is strictly greater than its neighbours:
• For the first element, compare with right neighbour only.
• For the last element, compare with left neighbour only.
• For all other elements, compare with both neighbours.
Approach: A single linear scan suffices. For each index, check the relevant neighbours
and collect the index if the condition holds.
• Time Complexity: O(n)
• Space Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of peak indices returned.

2.4. Question 4 — Query Problem
Medium · 14/20 TC
Problem Statement: Two types of queries on an array:
• Type 0: 0 i x — some update operation at index i with value x.
• Type 1: 1 x — some query on value x.
I don’t fully recall the exact semantics of the queries. My progressive approach:
1. Brute Force: Recompute from scratch for each query.

12/20 TC

3. Stage 2: Technical Interview
Date: 23rd October 2025
Mode: Online (video + shared coding platform)
Du-
ration: Approx. 50–55 minutes
Format: 1-on-1
HR Round: None
3.1. Introduction
The interview began with mutual introductions.
The interviewer was friendly and
approachable, creating a comfortable atmosphere.
I introduced myself and walked
through my academic background and interests. The interviewer also briefly shared his
own journey.
3.2. Project Discussion
One of my projects was discussed in depth — the interviewer went through it end to
end: why I chose to build it, what problem it solved, what my specific contributions were,
which model or algorithmic approach I used and why, and the trade-offs I considered. It
wasn’t a surface-level walkthrough; he probed every layer.
Tip: Be ready to defend every decision in your project — not just what you did, but
why. Know your model choices, architecture decisions, and what alternatives you
considered.
3.3. Coding Round — OOP + Binary Search
I was given a problem on a shared coding platform. It involved designing a class and
objects (OOP) and applying Binary Search on their attributes. Throughout the coding
session, the interviewer asked “why” questions about choices I made while writing the
code. I explained my reasoning at each step, and he was satisfied with the final output
and correctness.
3.4. DBMS Discussion
The interviewer shifted to Database Management Systems and asked about types of
keys. I covered the following:

Key Type
Description
Super Key
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tu-
ple in a relation.
Candidate Key
Minimal super key — no proper subset is also a
super key.
Primary Key
The chosen candidate key used to uniquely identify
each row.
Alternate Key
Candidate keys not chosen as the primary key.
Foreign Key
An attribute (or set) in one relation that references
the primary key of another relation.
Composite Key
A key consisting of two or more attributes.
3.5. Binary Search in DBMS — Indexing and B-Trees
The interviewer extended the Binary Search discussion to databases: “Where is Binary
Search used in DBMS?” I replied:
• Indexing: B-Trees and B+-Trees use a generalised form of binary search at each node
to navigate to the correct child pointer, enabling O(log n) lookups.
• B-Tree vs B+-Tree:
– In a B-Tree, data records can be stored at both internal and leaf nodes.
– In a B+-Tree, only leaf nodes store data; internal nodes store only keys. Leaf
nodes are linked in a list, enabling efficient range queries.
– Most modern RDBMS (MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL) use B+-Trees for clustered
and secondary indexes.
3.6. Questions to the Interviewer
I had researched VISA beforehand, which let me ask specific questions rooted in genuine
curiosity:
1. His experience and engineering culture at VISA — he spoke about the collab-
orative environment and the scale of problems the team works on.
2. Fraud detection at scale: How does VisaNet evaluate, flag, or allow a transaction
in milliseconds without adding noticeable latency for the end user? This sparked a
genuinely engaging conversation that he seemed to appreciate.
Tip for juniors: Research the company before your interview. Read about their
products, engineering challenges, or recent news. Questions that show you’ve done
your homework signal genuine curiosity and leave a strong impression.

Advice for Future Candidates
1. Strengthen DSA fundamentals.
2. Know your projects inside out. Every technology, every design decision, every
result — the interviewer will probe depth, not just breadth.
3. OOP is non-negotiable. Practice designing clean class hierarchies. Know encap-
sulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and when to use each.
4. DBMS matters much. At a company like VISA that handles billions of transac-
tions, understanding storage, indexing, and keys is directly relevant.
5. Communicate while coding. The interviewer asked “why” questions throughout.
Think out loud, explain your reasoning, and be open to hints.
6. Partial credit exists in OAs. Don’t give up. Brute force →optimise →submit.
7. Ask good questions at the end. It leaves a strong impression and makes the
conversation memorable for the interviewer.
All the best for your placements! Feel free to reach out if you have questions.
